paras: The threatened lynching of Hayes White took place in eastern Arkansas in April 1881, when armed posses and then a crowd at Forrest City sought White, a Black man accused of killing the sheriff of Crittenden County. White escaped the crowd when a train conductor hid him in the baggage car, and he was instead tried at Marion, convicted of first-degree murder, and hanged under court sentence on June 10, 1881. Newspapers widely expected him to be lynched, and the intent of the Forrest City crowd was later disputed.

According to the Memphis Appeal, White, described as a well-known resident near Crawfordsville, was captured on a Tuesday night in April while trying to force the safe of W. L. Trexell's store. After a hearing on Wednesday he was committed in default of bond and placed with a colored constable, Turner Hendrix (Hendricks), and a young white man, E. N. Sweepston, for the ride to the county jail at Marion. A few miles out, White drew a hidden pistol and shot the constable through the head, wounded Sweepston, and rode off after forcing him to give up his pistol.

On Thursday morning, April 21, Sheriff W. F. Beattie and Deputy Sheriff Maddox came to White's cabin, where Beattie was shot dead in the doorway and Maddox was wounded in the thigh. In a statement given to an Appeal reporter, White said he had been innocent of the burglary, shot Hendricks in anger after the constable refused to help him make bond, and fired at a man who snapped a gun at him in his house without knowing it was Beattie.

The Memphis wire of April 21 reported that a large posse of armed men was scouring Crittenden County and that White would be lynched if caught. The Appeal described squads of mounted colored and white men searching the country, while citizens offered a reward that the Public Ledger said had risen to more than $1,100. A party of six men from Forest City found White in a cabin ten miles below Augusta, but he walked away from them and escaped across White River. He was taken near Augusta about April 27 and put in irons; the Dallas Herald named ex-Sheriff M. W. Mason of Woodruff county as his captor, and White said he surrendered to Mason and four others.

On April 29, as White was being brought from Little Rock to Memphis by rail, a large crowd boarded the train at Forrest City, which the Appeal said came 'to Lynch White'. The conductor, Captain McDonald, had locked White in the baggage car and told the men he was in another car, and they left the train when it started. White was lodged overnight in the Memphis county jail before being returned to Marion.

White was tried in the Crittenden circuit court at Marion on May 3 before a jury of four white and eight colored men, after the court dismissed one defense attorney, James Phelan, for delaying the proceedings. He was convicted of first-degree murder, his counsel declined to appeal, and Judge Cypert sentenced him to death.

White was hanged at Marion on the afternoon of June 10 before a crowd of about 2,000; the drop did not break his neck and he strangled. A colored Baptist elder, H. G. Grundy, led hymns in which many Black spectators joined, and the body was given to his friends for burial.

Coverage came entirely from white papers, led by the Memphis Appeal, whose reporters supplied the local accounts, White's statement, the trial and the execution. Northern papers carried the Memphis wire under headlines such as 'A Negro Desperado's Deadly Work' and treated a lynching as likely, the Chicago Tribune reporting that 'Fears of Judge Lynch are expressed'. The Public Ledger wrote that White would be lucky to see the inside of the Marion jail, while a Chicago Tribune dispatch reported that whites and blacks had agreed to let him have a fair trial.

Arkansas papers followed the trial briefly; the Osceola Times mocked the deputy's flight, and the Batesville Guard wrote that justice had been promptly meted out. The Appeal described the hanging as the penalty demanded by the outraged law and stressed that the large mixed crowd caused no disturbance.

Five days after reporting the Forrest City episode, the Appeal printed a letter from a Forrest City citizen stating that lynching White was not contemplated by the men who boarded the train. Accounts also differ on the size of the Black crowd at the hanging, given as 1,500 of 2,000 by one wire, 500 by the Evening Star, and a thousand or more by the Appeal.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Hayes White
bases: The racial violence reported is a manhunt by armed posses and a crowd at Forrest City said to have boarded White's train to lynch him (A1, A5, A7, A8), which did not happen; White was tried, sentenced and legally hanged at Marion (A10, A12, A18, A19).

No one was lynched: the Forrest City crowd that the Appeal and a Memphis wire said meant to lynch White was evaded by the conductor (A7, A8), a Forrest City citizen denied any lynching was intended (A12), and White was hanged on June 10 under a court sentence (A18, A19).

The killings, capture, trial and legal hanging are reported by several independent papers (A3, A5, A10, A14, A18, A19), but the one mob threat, at Forrest City, is reported by the Appeal and a Memphis wire (A7, A8) and denied in a letter the Appeal printed (A12).

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the Memphis wire as 'A Negro Desperado's Deadly Work' and 'KILLED BY A BURGLAR', stating flatly that he would be lynched if caught.
The Memphis Public Ledger anticipated a lynching ('White will be lucky...'), while the Chicago wire stressed that whites and blacks had agreed to a fair trial.
The Memphis Appeal printed White's long statement, reported and then retracted the lynching intent, and called the hanging the penalty 'demanded by the outraged law'.
The Batesville Guard welcomed the conviction as justice 'promptly meted out'.
